Visitors explore an interactive Celestial Map featuring six real off-world landing sites—including the Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle, Laser Ranging Retroreflector, and Hasselblad Data Cameras on the Moon, alongside the Opportunity Rover, Ingenuity Helicopter, and InSight Lander on Mars. details:
What It Does & How It Works
Postcards from the Dust is an interactive, scrapbook-style digital museum built for the Abandoned but not Forgotten challenge. Visitors begin on an illustrated journal cover and open an interactive Celestial Map featuring six glowing location pins across the Moon and Mars. Clicking any pin opens a dedicated journal exhibit for a retired NASA artifact—including the Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle, Laser Ranging Retroreflector, and Hasselblad Data Cameras on the Moon, as well as the Opportunity Rover, Ingenuity Helicopter, and InSight Lander on Mars. Each exhibit combines official NASA photography, verified mission data, and built-in audio storytelling. Visitors can also explore an interactive 3D Rover Lab to rotate and zoom into official NASA 3D models of Opportunity, Perseverance, and Curiosity, sign the Visitor Guestbook, and preview upcoming exhibits in our future archive.

Benefits & Intended Impact
Technical space archives can sometimes feel overwhelming to younger students and the general public. By presenting NASA’s mission logs as personal stories, Postcards from the Dust makes space history accessible, emotional, and engaging for learners of all ages. Our intended impact is to shift how people view retired off-world hardware—not as "space junk," but as irreplaceable monuments of human curiosity that deserve protection as NASA prepares to return to the Moon with Artemis and send future missions to Mars.

How Our Project Is Creative
Instead of a traditional dark-tech dashboard, we designed the museum like a cozy, tactile travel scrapbook complete with crushed-paper textures, pastel lavender and baby-blue accents, washi tape, and tilted Polaroid frames. Blending multi-sensory elements—interactive map pins, audio narration, 3D model inspection, and a community guestbook—turns passive reading into an active journey of discovery.

Tools, Software & Resources Used

  • Design & Web Development: Built and deployed using Figma Make (generating interactive React, TypeScript, and CSS web components) and hosted live at https://figma.site.
  • AI Assistance: Used Google Gemini for research organization, museum exhibit storytelling, voiceover scriptwriting, and UI/UX prompt engineering.
  • Official NASA Data & Assets: Mission facts from NASA Science archives, photography from the NASA Image and Video Library, interactive 3D rover models from NASA 3D Resources / NASA Eyes, and preservation concepts from NASA’s Lunar Heritage Protection Guidelines.
  • Demo Production: Screen-captured with Windows Snipping Tool and edited with AI voiceover narration and captions in InShot.

Key Factors Considered
We prioritized scientific accuracy (verifying every date, distance, and mission outcome against official NASA records), accessibility (pairing audio guides with clear text and high-contrast typography), youth online safety (using AI voiceover narration rather than personal voice recordings), and scalability (designing a modular archive structure so future missions like Viking 1, Luna 9, and Spirit can be added easily).
